value.label: 1996 — Secure Environment for Untrusted Helper Applications
Sandbox vs virtualization
value.description: Sandboxing is a security mechanism; virtualization can provide a highly controlled environment but is broader.

value.label: Restricted OS vs full VM
value.description: A restricted process environment is distinct from a VM emulating a complete host computer.

value.label: Kernel mechanism vs policy
value.description: seccomp/cgroups/namespaces are listed Linux building blocks; rule-based frameworks impose access policy.

value.label: Android UID isolation
value.description: The described Android sandbox uses per-application Linux user IDs.

value.label: Jail vs VM
value.description: A jail is characterized by network and filesystem namespace restrictions rather than full hardware emulation.

value.label: Capabilities vs rules
value.description: Capabilities grant rights through tokens; rule-based systems assign access levels through rules.

value.label: OS vs instruction isolation
value.description: SFI constrains native instructions to memory segments.

value.label: Defense vs analysis
value.description: Sandboxing can contain threats and provide a controlled observation environment.

value.label: Restriction vs absolute denial
value.description: Resources may be disallowed or heavily restricted; sandboxing is not necessarily total denial.

value.label: Guest vs host
value.description: The sandbox boundary separates guest execution from host resources.

value.label: Security mechanism vs application container
value.description: The source presents sandboxing as a security mechanism and does not equate it with application containerization.

value.label: Trusted vs untrusted code
value.description: Sandboxing is especially useful for unverified/untrusted code.

value.label: Browser active code vs unrestricted code
value.description: Native Client and iframe sandboxing show active browser code can execute under restrictions.

value.label: Strict vs normal syscall surface
value.description: Strict seccomp exposes only four named system calls.

value.label: Embedded vs top-level content
value.description: HTML5 sandbox specifically constrains iframe content.

value.label: Platform-specific mechanisms
value.description: Linux, Android, Apple, Windows, browser and language runtimes use different mechanisms.

value.label: Virtual-hosting jail
value.description: Jails are noted as common in virtual hosting.

value.label: Fine-grained capability control
value.description: Capability systems are explicitly described as fine-grained sandboxing.

value.correction: The source treats VMs as one implementation and lists many non-VM mechanisms.
The source describes controlled, disallowed, or heavily restricted resources.
Online judges and pastebins are explicit non-malware use cases.

value.statement: Every app sandbox requires a VM
value.correction: Android's described mechanism uses Linux user IDs.
The source characterizes jails through network and filesystem namespace restrictions.
Tokens/capabilities grant specific rights; rule systems assign access levels.
The source includes browser, runtime, capability and instruction-level mechanisms.
SFI isolates specified native-code instruction effects into memory segments.

source_claims.statement: Sandbox separates running programs to mitigate spread of system failures and software vulnerabilities.
Sandbox resources include storage and memory scratch space; network access, host inspection and input-device access are usually restricted.
Sandboxing can be comparable to virtualization when providing a highly controlled environment.
Sandboxing is implemented by executing software in a restricted operating-system environment.
Linux application sandboxing uses seccomp, cgroups and namespaces.
Android assigns each application its own Linux user ID for application sandboxing.
GrapheneOS hardens app sandboxing and allows sandboxing every app as described.
Apple App Sandbox is required for specified App Store apps and recommended for other signed apps.
Virtual machines emulate a complete host computer and mediate host-resource access through the emulator.
Jails restrict network access and filesystem namespace and are common in virtual hosting.
Rule-based execution controls process spawning, code injection, network access and file/registry operations.
Security researchers use sandboxing to analyze malware behavior in replicated target environments.
Google Native Client sandboxes compiled C/C++ code in browsers independently of the user's OS.
Capability systems use opaque tokens to grant specific rights and can operate at kernel or user-space levels.
Strict seccomp permits only read, write, exit and sigreturn.
HTML5 iframe sandboxing restricts embedded content.
Java virtual machines sandbox untrusted applets/code.
.NET CLR Code Access Security restricts untrusted code.
SFI isolates store, read and jump assembly instructions into memory segments.
Online judges and executable pastebins are sandbox use cases.

value.title: Search engine
value.description: Full-detail structured knowledge graph based on the user-provided Wikipedia article about web search engines, including definitions, history, architecture, ranking, market context, bias, engine types, historical systems, and explicit relationships.

source_basis.primary_source: User-provided Wikipedia article text titled 'Search engine'
source_basis.scope_note: The supplied text is the source of the historical statements and figures below. Time-sensitive market-share figures are retained with their source date rather than represented as current.

value.definition: A search application that accepts a query and provides links to web pages and other relevant information, commonly with snippets, images, and specialized result types.
value.provider_architecture: A search engine can be one component of a distributed computing system spanning multiple data centers.

core_tasks.name: Find and select content
core_tasks.description: Discover full or partial content relevant to query terms.

core_tasks.name: Maintain an index
core_tasks.description: Store searchable representations and references to document locations.

core_tasks.name: Search the index
core_tasks.description: Match user queries against the index and return candidate documents.

core_tasks.name: Rank results
core_tasks.description: Order candidate results according to relevance and other system-specific signals.

core_tasks.name: Render results
core_tasks.description: Generate a results page with links, snippets, and potentially images or specialized modules.

value.important_distinction: A user query usually searches the search engine's index, not the live Web in its entirety.

processes.name: Web crawling
operations: follow links according to crawl policy
limitations: Some content is inaccessible to crawlers.
Crawl budgets and policies prevent exhaustive crawling of every reachable page.
Infinite URL spaces, spider traps, spam, and other practical issues constrain crawling.
Some sites are crawled extensively while others are only partially crawled.

processes.name: Indexing
operations: associate tokens with URLs or domain names
store searchable associations in index structures
update the index as pages change

processes.name: Query processing
operations: apply query operators and filters where supported
combine signals needed to rank results

processes.name: Ranking
processes.caveat: Ranking methods differ by engine and change over time; commercial implementations may treat parts of their methods as trade secrets.

processes.name: Result rendering
operations: render specialized result types when available

processes.name: Cache and refresh management
operations: retain some page content or renderable representations
serve stored representations between crawler visits
refresh data according to crawl schedules and policies
processes.caveat: A cached representation may differ from the live page if the page has changed since it was crawled.

robots_exclusion.function: Communicates crawl directives to compliant crawlers.
robots_exclusion.limitation: Crawl directives do not guarantee that all content is indexed or that every crawler will behave identically.

features: concept-based or statistically informed search in some systems
query_refinement.user_feedback_loop: Users refine queries and filters after reviewing initial results.

value.goal: Present useful, relevant, or authoritative results early in the result list.
signals_described_in_article: freshness or modification time where used

rankdex.claim: The article describes RankDex as an early search ranking system using hyperlinks to measure website quality.
rankdex.historical_significance: The article says RankDex preceded Google's similar PageRank patent filing and that Robin Li later used the technology in Baidu.

pagerank.principle: Uses the linking structure of the Web and the PageRank of linking pages to estimate relative importance.
pagerank.article_reported_influence: Larry Page's patent cited Robin Li's earlier RankDex work.

tradeoffs: Relevance is not identical to popularity.
Index coverage limits what can be retrieved.
Different engines can produce different results because they use different indexes and ranking algorithms.
Ranking methods and user-facing behavior evolve over time.

definition_and_core_functions.definition: A search application that accepts a query and provides links to web pages and other relevant information, commonly with snippets, images, and specialized result types.
definition_and_core_functions.provider_architecture: A search engine can be one component of a distributed computing system spanning multiple data centers.

core_tasks.name: Find and select content
core_tasks.description: Discover full or partial content relevant to query terms.

core_tasks.name: Maintain an index
core_tasks.description: Store searchable representations and references to document locations.

core_tasks.name: Search the index
core_tasks.description: Match user queries against the index and return candidate documents.

core_tasks.name: Rank results
core_tasks.description: Order candidate results according to relevance and other system-specific signals.

core_tasks.name: Render results
core_tasks.description: Generate a results page with links, snippets, and potentially images or specialized modules.

definition_and_core_functions.important_distinction: A user query usually searches the search engine's index, not the live Web in its entirety.

processes.name: Web crawling
operations: follow links according to crawl policy
limitations: Some content is inaccessible to crawlers.
Crawl budgets and policies prevent exhaustive crawling of every reachable page.
Infinite URL spaces, spider traps, spam, and other practical issues constrain crawling.
Some sites are crawled extensively while others are only partially crawled.

processes.name: Indexing
operations: associate tokens with URLs or domain names
store searchable associations in index structures
update the index as pages change

processes.name: Query processing
operations: apply query operators and filters where supported
combine signals needed to rank results

processes.name: Ranking
processes.caveat: Ranking methods differ by engine and change over time; commercial implementations may treat parts of their methods as trade secrets.

processes.name: Result rendering
operations: render specialized result types when available

processes.name: Cache and refresh management
operations: retain some page content or renderable representations
serve stored representations between crawler visits
refresh data according to crawl schedules and policies
processes.caveat: A cached representation may differ from the live page if the page has changed since it was crawled.

robots_exclusion.function: Communicates crawl directives to compliant crawlers.
robots_exclusion.limitation: Crawl directives do not guarantee that all content is indexed or that every crawler will behave identically.

features: concept-based or statistically informed search in some systems
query_refinement.user_feedback_loop: Users refine queries and filters after reviewing initial results.

ranking_and_relevance.goal: Present useful, relevant, or authoritative results early in the result list.
signals_described_in_article: freshness or modification time where used

rankdex.claim: The article describes RankDex as an early search ranking system using hyperlinks to measure website quality.
rankdex.historical_significance: The article says RankDex preceded Google's similar PageRank patent filing and that Robin Li later used the technology in Baidu.

pagerank.principle: Uses the linking structure of the Web and the PageRank of linking pages to estimate relative importance.
pagerank.article_reported_influence: Larry Page's patent cited Robin Li's earlier RankDex work.

tradeoffs: Relevance is not identical to popularity.
Index coverage limits what can be retrieved.
Different engines can produce different results because they use different indexes and ranking algorithms.
Ranking methods and user-facing behavior evolve over time.

pre_web_precursors.description: The article states that Internet user-search systems predate the Web and dates WHOIS search to 1982.

value.label: System image vs process image

value.label: Persistent vs volatile state
value.description: Images make otherwise volatile execution state recoverable.

value.label: Hibernation vs backup
value.description: Hibernation is a specific RAM-state persistence operation; backup is a broader purpose.

value.label: Savestate vs backup
value.description: Savestate preserves emulated execution state; the source does not equate it with general backup.

value.label: Migration vs restoration
value.description: Migration transfers state to another machine; restoration reconstructs prior state.

value.label: Lisp image vs database dump
value.description: Both persist state, but Lisp images can combine executable code and application data.

value.label: World vs incremental World
value.description: Full World contains OS/apps/data; incremental World contains changes from a base.

value.label: System image vs core dump
value.description: Similar structure does not imply identical purpose.

value.label: Image vs source code
value.description: An image may contain compiled/customized runtime state rather than source text.

value.label: Image distribution vs rebuild
value.description: Distribution of initialized images avoids repeated startup initialization.

value.label: Runtime state vs program artifact
value.description: Image can combine executable code, application data, and runtime state.

Smalltalk and Lisp support system images; Lisp can preserve compiled/customized code and loaded data.
Executable images can be distributed to avoid repeated initialization.
Lisp Machines boot from Worlds containing OS, applications, and data; incremental Worlds store changes.
System images resemble core dumps structurally but have different purposes.

value.name: Encapsulation
value.expression: application data → transport unit → IP datagram → link frame → medium
value.meaning: Data gains protocol context while descending the stack.

value.name: Decapsulation
value.expression: medium → frame → IP datagram → transport data → application

value.name: IP forwarding
value.expression: destination IP → routing decision → next hop → repeated forwarding → destination

value.name: TCP reliability
value.expression: connection + ordering + retransmission + flow control + congestion control
value.meaning: TCP supplies reliable transport over IP.

value.name: UDP service
value.expression: application data → UDP datagram → IP → link

value.name: Endpoint addressing
value.expression: IP address + transport port → application endpoint

value.name: End-to-end architecture
value.meaning: Core forwards; endpoints provide broader intelligence/reliability.

value.name: TCP/IP and OSI mapping
value.expression: TCP/IP application≈OSI session+presentation+application; transport≈transport; internet≈network; link≈data-link/physical boundary

value.name: NFS example stack
value.expression: NFS → XDR → RPC → UDP → IP → Link

value.name: Implementation stack
value.expression: application → transport → IP → link driver/firmware/chipset → medium
value.meaning: Abstract protocol layers connect to concrete network hardware.

value.name: Historical convergence
value.expression: ARPANET/NCP → internetworking research → TCP/IP → 1983 migration → adoption
value.meaning: Research and deployment produced the dominant Internet suite.

value.distinction: TCP/IP is an Internet architecture; OSI is a seven-layer general reference model.
IP provides internetworking; TCP provides reliable transport.
TCP is connection-oriented/reliable; UDP is connectionless/best-effort.
IP addresses identify hosts/locations; ports identify service channels.
IP packets are carried inside local link frames.
Layering defines scopes; encapsulation wraps data across those scopes.
End-to-end concerns endpoint intelligence; layering concerns functional separation.
IPv6 expands addresses from 32 to 128 bits.
Gateway was an earlier term for router.
QUIC is a transport protocol carried by UDP.
User protocols serve applications; support protocols serve infrastructure.
IP/UDP provide best-effort while TCP/SCTP can provide reliability.
TCP/IP link/physical correspondence varies by representation.
IETF routing protocols carried over IP can be categorized as application-layer protocols in the cited TCP/IP treatment.

value.misconception: TCP/IP has seven layers exactly like OSI.
value.correction: TCP/IP's standard four-layer representation differs from OSI.
IP is best-effort; reliability can be added above it.

value.misconception: TCP and IP are the same protocol.
value.correction: TCP is transport; IP is internetworking.
UDP uses a checksum for error detection.

value.misconception: A port is another IP address.
value.correction: A port identifies a logical communication channel/service.
Routers generally forward encapsulated traffic without application interpretation.

value.misconception: TCP/IP defines a mandatory separate physical layer.
value.correction: Physical details may be implicit below the link layer.
HTTP/3 works exclusively through QUIC, which is carried over UDP.

value.misconception: IPv6 is just a faster IPv4.
value.correction: The source emphasizes IPv6's expanded 128-bit addressing to address exhaustion.

value.misconception: End-to-end means there are no middleboxes.
value.correction: The source explicitly notes firewalls, NATs and caches changed the original assumption.

formal_models.name: Decapsulation
formal_models.expression: medium → frame → IP datagram → transport data → application

formal_models.meaning: TCP supplies reliable transport over IP.

formal_models.name: UDP service
formal_models.expression: application data → UDP datagram → IP → link

formal_models.name: Endpoint addressing

formal_models.name: End-to-end architecture

formal_models.name: Implementation stack
formal_models.expression: application → transport → IP → link driver/firmware/chipset → medium

formal_models.meaning: Research and deployment produced the dominant Internet suite.

source_claims.claim: TCP/IP organizes communication into four functional layers and specifies packetization, addressing, transmission, routing and reception.
IETF maintains the suite's technical standards and the suite predates OSI.
DARPA-sponsored ARPANET research and BBN IMPs formed early infrastructure.
Kahn and Cerf hid differences among local networks and delegated reliability to hosts.
The 1978 reformulation separated TCP and IP into distinct transport and internetwork functions.
End-to-end design, encapsulation and layering are central architectural principles.
IPv4/TCP-IP became active on ARPANET in 1983 and DoD standardized TCP/IP for military networking.
Transport provides channels, ports, reliability, segmentation, flow/congestion control and multiple protocol choices.
Application protocols include both user and support protocols and usually treat lower layers as abstractions.
TCP/IP and OSI use different layer representations and IETF does not require strict OSI compliance.
TCP/IP is hardware independent and has implementations across essentially every computing platform.
Minimal implementations include IP, ARP, ICMP, TCP, UDP and IGMP; IPv6 adds NDP and ICMPv6 among its support protocols.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: TCP/IP is an Internet architecture; OSI is a seven-layer general reference model.
IP provides internetworking; TCP provides reliable transport.
TCP is connection-oriented/reliable; UDP is connectionless/best-effort.
IP addresses identify hosts/locations; ports identify service channels.
IP packets are carried inside local link frames.
Layering defines scopes; encapsulation wraps data across those scopes.
End-to-end concerns endpoint intelligence; layering concerns functional separation.
IPv6 expands addresses from 32 to 128 bits.
Gateway was an earlier term for router.
QUIC is a transport protocol carried by UDP.
User protocols serve applications; support protocols serve infrastructure.
IP/UDP provide best-effort while TCP/SCTP can provide reliability.
TCP/IP link/physical correspondence varies by representation.
IETF routing protocols carried over IP can be categorized as application-layer protocols in the cited TCP/IP treatment.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP/IP has seven layers exactly like OSI.
misconceptions.correction: TCP/IP's standard four-layer representation differs from OSI.
IP is best-effort; reliability can be added above it.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP and IP are the same protocol.
misconceptions.correction: TCP is transport; IP is internetworking.
UDP uses a checksum for error detection.

misconceptions.misconception: A port is another IP address.
misconceptions.correction: A port identifies a logical communication channel/service.
Routers generally forward encapsulated traffic without application interpretation.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP/IP defines a mandatory separate physical layer.
misconceptions.correction: Physical details may be implicit below the link layer.
HTTP/3 works exclusively through QUIC, which is carried over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 is just a faster IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: The source emphasizes IPv6's expanded 128-bit addressing to address exhaustion.

misconceptions.misconception: End-to-end means there are no middleboxes.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly notes firewalls, NATs and caches changed the original assumption.

value.summary: Detailed machine-readable graph of Tor's purpose, onion routing, relay roles, circuits, onion services, history, software ecosystem, privacy use cases, threat model, attacks and limitations, and source provenance.

value.primary_input: User-supplied text of the Wikipedia article 'Tor (network)', redirected from 'Tor (anonymity network)'
value.method: Core claims are derived from the supplied article. Additional current documentation and technical explanations are explicitly marked as external references or background context.
value.version_freshness_warning: The supplied article contains version and network-size snapshots that can change quickly. Do not treat version numbers, relay counts, user counts, or legal/political descriptions as current unless independently checked against current official sources.
limitations: Tor is an anonymity-enhancing system, not a guarantee of absolute anonymity.
Low-latency routing cannot reliably defeat an adversary able to observe and correlate traffic at both ends.
Traffic from applications not routed through Tor Browser or a configured Tor proxy is not automatically protected.
Tor does not itself provide end-to-end encryption between an exit relay and a public Internet destination; use HTTPS or another end-to-end encrypted protocol.
Historical attack descriptions and statistics are included as claims reported by the supplied article, not as independently verified current findings.

value.event: Alpha version of Tor launched as The Onion Routing project
Onion services first specified, according to the supplied article
First public release of Tor, approximately one year after the alpha launch
Naval Research Laboratory released Tor code under a free license; EFF supported continued development
Onion services began deployment on the Tor network, according to the supplied article
The Tor Project was founded as a nonprofit organization
Tor Project disclosed a relay-early traffic-confirmation attack involving malicious relays; affected relays were removed and software was patched, according to the supplied article

public_internet_circuit.component: client application configured to use Tor
public_internet_circuit.action: The application sends supported TCP traffic to a local Tor SOCKS interface or Tor Browser.
The first relay receives traffic from the client; it can see the client's network address but ordinarily not the final destination.
Forwards the circuit to the next hop without being the public Internet exit.
Removes the final Tor relay layer and connects to the public Internet destination; destination typically sees the exit IP.
Receives the request. If the application protocol lacks end-to-end encryption, traffic between exit and destination may be observable or modifiable.

onion_service_connection.action: Knows or obtains the service's .onion address and uses Tor-capable software.
Client obtains service connection information through Tor's distributed directory mechanisms.
Client chooses a path through Tor, including a rendezvous point.
Onion service independently builds a Tor path and connects to the rendezvous point.
Joins the circuits; communication remains within Tor and does not use a public Internet exit.

value.important_distinction: Tor routes traffic through relays; it is not a replacement for HTTPS, secure endpoint configuration, or sound operational security.

protected_properties: reduce destination visibility of the client's ordinary public IP
reduce any single relay's ability to see both source and destination
support location privacy and censorship circumvention
support onion services without publishing the host's ordinary IP address
out_of_scope_or_limited_properties: perfect anonymity against global or multi-point traffic observation
protection from malware or a compromised operating system
preventing identification when a user logs into a personal account or reveals identifying details
automatically routing every application on a device through Tor
end-to-end encryption between exit relay and public destination when the application does not provide it
preventing a destination from recognizing or blocking Tor exit IP addresses
attacker_capabilities_to_consider: control or observation of one relay
observation by an ISP or local network
simultaneous observation of traffic entering and leaving Tor
operation of multiple malicious relays (Sybil behavior)
blocking public relays or Tor traffic
mitigations_and_hygiene: Use the official Tor Browser or correctly configured applications.
Keep software updated and obtain it from official project sources.
Use HTTPS for public Internet websites.
Do not assume other applications on the device are routed through Tor.
Avoid logging into identifying accounts when identity separation is the goal.
Do not open downloaded documents in an application that can make unprotected network requests while the user is online unless the risks are understood.
Use bridges or supported pluggable transports where appropriate for censorship circumvention.
Use official Tor Project documentation for current configuration advice.
